conflicts/munster-rebellion/religionRole: Few conflicts were more thoroughly religious. The Anabaptist takeover was driven by Melchior Hoffman's prophecy of the imminent end and by Jan Matthys's conviction that the elect must now wield the sword to prepare the New Jerusalem; the besieging prince-bishop fought to recover his city and to destroy heresy, supported by Lutheran and Catholic princes alike. Historians (Sigrun Haude, Ralf Klötzer, James Stayer) also stress the background of guild politics, the struggle of the city against its bishop, and the influx of desperate refugees from the Netherlands, but they agree that apocalyptic belief was the motor of events.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/sides/1/name: Prince-Bishop of Münster and allied princes
conflicts/munster-rebellion/sides/1/lead: Archbishop Hermann von Wied of Cologne
conflicts/munster-rebellion/summary: In 1534 radical Anabaptists, expecting the imminent return of Christ, took control of the Westphalian city of Münster, expelled those who refused rebaptism and proclaimed it the New Jerusalem. Under siege by its Catholic prince-bishop and Lutheran allies, the city became a theocratic kingdom with community of goods, polygamy and a self-proclaimed King David, Jan of Leiden. It fell in June 1535 amid famine and massacre, and its memory haunted Anabaptists and justified their persecution for generations.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/story:
Münster was the seat of a prince-bishopric whose citizens, organised in powerful guilds, had long struggled against their clerical overlord. From 1531 the preacher Bernhard Rothmann won the city for the Reformation, and the Treaty of Dülmen in February 1533 granted the parish churches to the evangelicals. Rothmann soon moved beyond Lutheranism, rejecting infant baptism and adopting a symbolic view of the Lord's Supper. At the same time the Low Countries were full of followers of Melchior Hoffman, a lay preacher who taught that the last days were at hand and that Strasbourg would be the New Jerusalem in 1533; when Hoffman was imprisoned there, his follower Jan Matthys, a baker from Haarlem, claimed to be the prophet Enoch, declared that the time of patient suffering was over, and transferred the hope of the New Jerusalem to Münster.

In January 1534 Matthys's ‘apostles’ arrived in Münster and rebaptised some 1,400 people within a week; among them was a young tailor from Leiden, Jan Bockelson. Anabaptists flowed in from the region and the Netherlands, while Catholics and Lutherans left. On 23 February 1534 the Anabaptists won the council elections and the cloth merchant Bernhard Knipperdolling became burgomaster. Matthys arrived, and on 27 February all who refused rebaptism were driven out of the city into a winter storm, leaving their property behind. Prince-Bishop Franz von Waldeck began a siege the next day. In March some 3,000 Dutch Anabaptists who sailed for Münster were intercepted near Hasselt and Genemuiden, and their leaders executed.

Inside the walls Matthys ordered all property held in common, money abolished and every book except the Bible burned. On Easter Sunday, 5 April 1534, believing himself called to be a new Gideon, he rode out with a handful of men against the besiegers and was killed. Jan of Leiden took over, replaced the council with twelve elders after the tribes of Israel, and repelled major assaults on 25 May and 31 August 1534. In July he introduced polygamy, justified by the patriarchs and by the surplus of women in the city; an uprising led by the smith Heinrich Mollenhecke was crushed and its participants executed. In September Jan was proclaimed King of the New Jerusalem, with a court, crown and orb, as the ruler of the whole world before Christ's return.

Rothmann's tracts The Restitution (October 1534) and On Vengeance (December 1534) called on true Christians everywhere to take up the sword against the godless. Emissaries were sent out to raise the faithful, and in 1535 Melchiorite risings broke out in the Netherlands: some 300 Anabaptists seized the Oldeklooster near Bolsward in Friesland in March–April 1535 and were killed or executed when it was stormed, and on 10–11 May an attack on Amsterdam's town hall ended in executions. Within Münster discipline was savage; dissenters, deserters and disobedient wives were executed, and Jan himself was said to have beheaded one of his wives, Elisabeth Wandscherer, in the market square.

By the spring of 1535 the blockade, now supported by princes of the Empire, Lutheran and Catholic, had brought famine; people ate grass, rats and leather. Jan let starving women, children and old men leave, but many were killed or left to die between the lines. On the night of 24–25 June 1535 two deserters, including Heinrich Gresbeck, guided the besiegers through a weak point in the walls. Hundreds of defenders were killed in the fighting and the massacre that followed; others were executed, and the women were expelled. Rothmann disappeared and was probably killed. Jan of Leiden, Knipperdolling and Bernhard Krechting were displayed around the region, then publicly tortured with red-hot tongs and executed on 22 January 1536; their bodies were hung in iron cages from the tower of St Lambert's Church, where the cages still hang.

Münster was restored to Catholicism under the bishop. Across Europe ‘Münster’ became a byword used by Catholics and Protestants to justify the persecution of all Anabaptists as seditious. Among the survivors of the Melchiorite movement, a violent fringe continued under Jan van Batenburg, but the majority were regathered by Obbe and Dirk Philips and by the former priest Menno Simons, who rejected the sword and the kingdom of Münster and built the peaceful communities later called Mennonites.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/nameOfGod: The Münsterites believed they were living in the last days foretold in Daniel and Revelation, that Münster was the New Jerusalem and Matthys the prophet Enoch, and that the elect must purify the earth of the godless before Christ's return. Rothmann's On Vengeance (1534) told Christians that the time had come to ‘repay Babylon double’. Jan of Leiden ruled as a new King David, and his throne bore an orb pierced by two swords. On the other side the bishop and princes fought to suppress heresy and sedition, and the imperial authorities invoked the 1529 Diet of Speyer's mandate imposing death on rebaptisers.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/religiousCau: Melchior Hoffman's prophecy that the end of the world would come in 1533 and that 144,000 witnesses would gather in the New Jerusalem.
Jan Matthys's teaching that the time of suffering was over and that the elect must take the sword against the ungodly.
Bernhard Rothmann's radicalisation of the Münster Reformation, rejecting infant baptism and the authority of the bishop.
The bishop's and princes' determination to destroy Anabaptism, which imperial law since 1529 punished with death.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/otherCauses/: A long struggle between the city's guilds and its prince-bishop over civic autonomy.
The persecution of Anabaptists in the Habsburg Netherlands, which drove thousands of refugees to seek a place of safety.
Economic distress among artisans and the urban poor in the Low Countries and Westphalia in the early 1530s.
The fear of princes, Lutheran and Catholic, that a successful ‘revolution of the saints’ would spread throughout the Empire.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/triggers/0: The arrival of Jan Matthys's apostles and the mass rebaptisms of January 1534.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/triggers/1: The Anabaptist victory in the council elections of 23 February 1534 and the expulsion of non-Anabaptists on 27 February.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/triggers/2: Prince-Bishop Franz von Waldeck's decision to besiege the city.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/0/t: Treaty of Dülmen (February) gives Münster's parish churches to the evangelicals; Rothmann rejects infant baptism; Hoffman is imprisoned in Strasbourg.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/1/t: 5 January: Matthys's apostles arrive and begin mass rebaptism; Jan of Leiden arrives a week later.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/2/t: 23 February: Anabaptists win the council elections; 27 February: non-Anabaptists are expelled and the siege begins.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/3/t: March: some 3,000 Dutch Anabaptists sailing to Münster are intercepted near Hasselt.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/4/t: 5 April: Matthys is killed in a sortie on Easter Sunday; Jan of Leiden takes control.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/5/t: 25 May and 31 August: major assaults by the besiegers are repelled.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/6/t: July: polygamy is introduced and the Mollenhecke revolt crushed; September: Jan is crowned king.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/7/t: October–December: Rothmann's Restitution and On Vengeance call for holy war.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/8/t: March–April: Anabaptists seize and lose the Oldeklooster in Friesland; May: attack on Amsterdam town hall.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/9/t: 24–25 June: Münster is taken by treachery and its defenders massacred.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/10/: 22 January: Jan of Leiden, Knipperdolling and Krechting are tortured and executed; their bodies are hung in cages on St Lambert's tower.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/timeline/11/: Menno Simons leaves the Catholic priesthood and begins to regather peaceful Anabaptists.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/0/: Claimed to be Enoch, sent apostles to rebaptise, made Münster the New Jerusalem and introduced community of goods.
Killed in a sortie against the besiegers on Easter Sunday 1534.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/1/: Succeeded Matthys, introduced polygamy and ruled as a messianic king during the siege.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/2/: Cloth merchant, burgomaster and later executioner of the kingdom
Led the Anabaptist party among the citizens and enforced Jan's discipline.
Executed with Jan of Leiden in 1536.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/3/: Led the city from Lutheranism to Anabaptism and wrote the kingdom's propaganda, including On Vengeance.
Disappeared when the city fell, probably killed.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/4/: His prophecies inspired the movement, though he himself taught that believers should wait passively for God.
Died in prison in Strasbourg after about ten years' confinement.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/5/: Besieged the city for sixteen months with help from the Empire's princes.
Recovered and re-Catholicised the city; himself later flirted with the Reformation.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/6/: Escaped and guided the besiegers into the city in June 1535.
Wrote an eyewitness account of the kingdom, an important source alongside Hermann von Kerssenbrock's hostile history.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/keyPeople/7/: Shaken by the deaths of Münsterites at the Oldeklooster, among them probably his brother, he wrote against Jan of Leiden's ‘blasphemy’.
Left the priesthood in 1536 and led the non-violent Anabaptists who took his name.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/casualties/n: No reliable totals exist. The city's population during the siege is estimated at roughly 7,000–9,000, many of them women. Several hundred defenders were killed in the storming of June 1535 and in the executions that followed, and an unknown number died of hunger or were killed between the lines during the famine. Besiegers' losses in the failed assaults of 1534 ran to hundreds. Hundreds more Melchiorites were executed in the Netherlands and Westphalia in 1534–36, after the Oldeklooster and Amsterdam risings and in the wider persecution.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/effects/0: Münster was restored to the prince-bishop and to Catholicism, and lost much of its civic independence.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/effects/1: Imperial and territorial authorities intensified the persecution of all Anabaptists, citing Münster as proof of their sedition.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/effects/2: The episode became a stock example in European political thought of the dangers of religious ‘enthusiasm’ and fanaticism.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/effectsOnChu: Anabaptism split decisively between a violent apocalyptic fringe, which faded after the 1530s, and a pacifist majority led by Menno Simons and the Philips brothers.
Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic polemic for centuries equated believers' baptism with revolution, making Münster a burden on Mennonites and later Baptists.
The Mennonite tradition of non-resistance and separation from political power was shaped in conscious reaction to Münster.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/legacy: The cages on St Lambert's tower remain the most visible memorial of the kingdom. For Mennonites, Münster was a trauma that confirmed the path of non-violence; for Catholic and Protestant authorities it justified the persecution of peaceable Anabaptists for generations. Modern historians read it as an extreme case of apocalyptic expectation under siege rather than as typical of Anabaptism, and in 2025 the city and churches of Münster joined Mennonites in reflecting on the persecution that followed.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/dissenters/0: In a tract against ‘the blasphemy of Jan of Leiden’ (c. 1535) he denied that any Christian king but Christ could rule his kingdom, and taught that believers ‘beat their swords into ploughshares’ and must never fight with the sword.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/dissenters/1: A Melchiorite elder who rejected Matthys's claims and the resort to arms, and gathered the peaceful Anabaptists of the Netherlands before handing leadership to Menno.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/dissenters/2: Although his prophecies set events in motion, Hoffman himself taught that the godly should wait for God's judgement rather than take up the sword.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/theatres/3/n: Interception of the Anabaptist fleet near Hasselt
conflicts/munster-rebellion/campaigns/0/: The road to the New Jerusalem
Jan Matthys's apostles and Dutch Anabaptist refugees
From Haarlem Matthys sent pairs of apostles through the Dutch provinces to rebaptise and to summon the faithful to Münster; the first arrived on 5 January 1534 and Matthys followed in February.
conflicts/munster-rebellion/campaigns/1/: Answering Matthys's summons, some 3,000 Anabaptists in about 27 ships crossed the Zuiderzee intending to march to Münster; they were stopped by the authorities of Overijssel at the mouth of the Zwarte Water, and most were sent home while their leaders were executed.
